children.text: A scattering of limestone islands and white sandbars off the Caramoan Peninsula in the Bicol region, explored by bangka boat. Known as a filming location for Survivor franchises from several countries, it remains uncrowded, making it ideal for travelers who want a raw island landscape completely different from Boracay.

Caramoan is the name given to both the peninsula at the eastern tip of Camarines Sur, in the Bicol region in southeastern Luzon, and the islands off its coast. Facing Lagonoy Gulf on the Pacific side, the area has dozens of small islands where sharp limestone peaks rise from the sea, each holding a short but fine sandy beach and shallow emerald-colored water. Because it sits at the end of a peninsula cut off from the mainland, transport was inconvenient for a long time, which slowed development — even now, simple homestays and family-run resorts outnumber large resorts.
Administratively, Caramoan is a municipality covering about 276 km² with 49 barangays and about 50,000 people (2024 census), located about
110 km
from Naga by road. Tradition holds that the Spanish missionary Francisco de la Cruz opened the first settlement in the interior of the peninsula in
, and the peninsula's limestone terrain, forests, and caves were designated Caramoan National Park in
. The US version of Survivor filmed season 25, "Philippines," and season 26, "Caramoan," here, which aired in
and
, and the French version, "Koh-Lanta," aired a season filmed in
April–May 2025
in the spring of
. Access is restricted during filming: from
April 15–July 22, 2016
, Gota Village Resort and several islands, including Sabitang Laya, Lahos, and Matukad, were closed, but well-known islands such as Manlawi, Cotivas, and Tinago stayed open.
What brought this place to the world's attention was a reality survival show. From around

, the French, Israeli, Bulgarian, and other national versions of "Survivor" were filmed here, and the US version aired its season 26 as "Survivor: Caramoan." Some islands and beaches are off-limits while filming is underway, but at other times you can tour filming-location islands such as Matukad Island, Lahos Island, and Sabitang Laya by bangka.

Caramoan town still has a stone church built in the Spanish era, and on top of the nearby limestone peak Mount Caglago stands a statue of the Virgin Mary overlooking the sea — a chance to feel the deeply Catholic atmosphere of the Bicol region as well. Bicolano food built on coconut milk and hot chilies adds to the pleasure of the trip.

It suits travelers who prefer quiet island hopping, snorkeling, and sandbar walks over crowded famous beaches, and those willing to put up with somewhat inconvenient transport to see the Philippines in a more original form. Travelers expecting amenities and nightlife may be disappointed.

Chartering a single bangka to visit 4–6 islands in a day is the heart of a Caramoan trip. Tours are split into near-island and far-island routes, and the per-person cost drops sharply once enough people join.
A small island ringed by limestone cliffs — climb over a gap in the rocks and a secret lagoon connected to the sea appears. The rocks are sharp, so wearing aqua shoes is a good idea.
At low tide, white sandbars emerge on both sides of the island, giving the feeling of walking through the middle of the sea. It is one of the islands best known as a Survivor filming location.

blocks.title: Snorkeling at Sabitang Laya and Cagbalinad

children.text: The shallow, clear water makes it easy to see coral and tropical fish. It's best to visit in the morning when the waves are calm.
Climb hundreds of steps to the summit and the islands off Caramoan spread out before you. It's best to climb early in the morning before the sun gets hot.
A quiet beach on the peninsula side, with a resort once used as the Survivor production team's base and a small cove beneath the cliffs. A good spot to watch the sunset after island hopping.
Bicol Express (pork simmered in coconut milk and chilies), laing (taro leaves stewed in coconut milk), and pili nut snacks are must-tries in this region.

blocks.title: St. Michael the Archangel Church and a stroll around town

children.text: A red-brick church in Caramoan town (Tawog district). The parish was founded in

, and the present building is made of stone and mud brick. The arched entrance, the niches holding statues of saints, and the bell tower are worth a look. The Isla Carahan festival is said to be held on the parish feast day,
May 8
. It takes about
20–30 minutes
to look around after island hopping.

; have lunch here

Naga Airport (WNP) is in Pili, about
30 minutes
from Naga city. Because small propeller aircraft were banned from Manila airport, there have been no direct Manila–Naga flights since
March 29, 2026
, and now Cebu Pacific (Cebgo) flies the Clark–Naga route. One-way fares are about

depending on the season. If flying from Manila, you can also fly to Bicol International Airport (DRP), which has jet service, and continue overland via Naga, but the travel time to Caramoan is longer.
Several buses a day run from terminals in Manila such as Cubao and Pasay to Naga, taking about
8–10 hours
and costing about
(regular to sleeper bus). From the Naga Central Bus Terminal, air-conditioned buses to Caramoan, such as Florencia, MRR, and Raymond, run from dawn until early afternoon, taking about
4–5 hours
and costing about
. The road follows the Huyentebela national highway over coast and mountains.
To go from Manila without transferring, take a direct air-conditioned bus to Caramoan such as Raymond or Peñafrancia. It departs in the afternoon or evening and arrives the next morning, taking about
11–14 hours
and costing about
. Departure terminals and times change often, so check in advance.
The Raymond bus timetable lists Caramoan departures at
and
(from Cubao), while other guides say they leave at
6–8 PM
. The operator states that schedules can change without notice, so confirm the departure time when you book.
Old guidebooks say a scheduled passenger bangka runs from Sabang Port (San Jose) to Caramoan's Guijalo Port, taking about
2 hours
and costing about
. However,

sources and local tour operators say this scheduled service no longer exists. Don't plan on waiting for a boat at Sabang Port; if you need a boat, check with your accommodation in advance whether a chartered bangka is available.
The Caramoan environmental fee is about
per person, paid at the Paniman Beach reception desk (or Guijalo Port) before island hopping. From Guijalo Port to town or your accommodation, a tricycle takes about
20–30 minutes
and costs about
per tricycle.
From Virac Airport (VRC), travel overland about
30–45 minutes
to a port on the San Andres side (such as Codon), then cross the Maqueda Channel by chartered bangka to reach Caramoan. The crossing takes about
1 hour
and a charter costs about
. Boats are hard to run when waves are high, so check the weather. The island itself can be seen separately at
Catanduanes
It is about
110 km
from Naga along the Huyentebela national highway, a trip that takes
4–5 hours
by bus. The road has sharp curves, unlit stretches, and coastal cliff roads, so leave in time to arrive before sunset.
For island hopping, charter a bangka through your accommodation or the tourist information office. Near-island routes cost around
per boat, and far-island routes around
. Get around town by tricycle.
The island-hopping departure point is Paniman Beach, a
15–20 minutes
tricycle ride from town, costing about
per tricycle. Most certified bangkas are based here, and you pay the environmental fee and register at the reception desk. A tricycle within town costs about
per person.
Caramoan faces the Pacific on the eastern side of the Philippines, so its weather pattern differs from west-coast destinations. From
November
to
February
, the northeast monsoon (Amihan) brings frequent rain and high waves, and there are many days when boats are cancelled or island hopping is called off.
The best time is from
March
to
June
. There is little rain and the sea is calm, making it good for reaching the far islands, and the water is at its clearest. However, during Holy Week (
March–April
) and the summer school break, local Filipino travelers crowd in, so book accommodation ahead.
July
to
October

is the rainy season and typhoon season. Bicol lies along a frequent typhoon path, so during this period you must check PAGASA forecasts. During the Peñafrancia Festival held in Naga around the third week of
September
, accommodation in downtown Naga fills up, but it's also a good chance to see genuine Bicolano culture.
Midday temperatures in Caramoan are around
year-round, and annual rainfall is about 2,763 mm with no distinct dry season. So judge the weather by sea conditions rather than rain. The far-island itinerary is most reliable from
March–May
, and from
October–January
, when the northeast monsoon blows, waves are high and cancellations are frequent. The fluvial procession of the Peñafrancia Festival in Naga takes place on the afternoon of
September 19, 2026
(a Saturday), and roads in the city are closed from noon that day, so allow extra time if you are changing buses in Naga around then.

Accommodation falls broadly into two types: Caramoan town (the Poblacion) and beachfront resorts. The town has guesthouses and homestays clustered together at about

per night, convenient for restaurants, the market, and getting to the port. Island-hopping bangkas are also easy to arrange through town accommodations. Along the coast, resorts around Gota Beach and Tugawe Cove sit right on the water, at
or more per night, often sold as packages bundling meals with island hopping.

The food centers on Bicolano cuisine. Bicol Express (simmered in coconut milk and chilies), laing (dried taro leaves stewed in coconut milk), and ginataang gulay (vegetables cooked in coconut milk) are typical, and generally spicy. Being a seaside town, grilled fish, squid, and crab dishes are cheap. On island-hopping days, it's common to ask your accommodation the day before to prepare a packed lunch or barbecue, or to buy seafood at the town market and have the bangka boatman grill it. If you pass through Naga, pili-nut cookies and candies make good souvenirs.
Choosing accommodation by how easy it is to get around is simplest. The Paniman Beach area (Paniman Bay Lodge and others) costs about
per night and is close to the reception desk, and in town La Casa Roa Hostel costs about
. A leading upscale option is Tugawe Cove Resort in Colongcogon on the north of the peninsula, at about

per night depending on the room. Gota Village Resort on Gota Beach is closed during filming, so check before booking. For meals, Caramotan Grill (grilled squid) on Paniman Beach and Caramoan Bed and Dine (Bicol Express) in town are often mentioned, and market eateries cost
or less per meal. Many kitchens close by
8 PM
, so eat dinner early.
Caramoan has almost no ATMs, and the few that exist often break down, so it's safer to withdraw all the cash you'll need in downtown Naga. Only the larger resorts tend to accept card payments.
Smart and Globe signals reach the town but are weak or absent on the islands and outlying beaches. If you need data, it's a good idea to carry SIM cards from both carriers.
Island hopping gets cheaper with more people, so it's worth asking your accommodation about joining other travelers to share a bangka.
The rocks at Matukad Island and the reef beaches are sharp, so aqua shoes are essential. Snorkel gear can be rented at your accommodation, but bringing your own is more hygienic.
Boats from Sabang Port mostly run in the morning, so taking a van that leaves Naga at dawn makes same-day arrival easier. If you're running late, it's better to switch to the direct overland bus.
The sandbar and Lahos Island look best at low tide, so it's a good idea to check a tide table before you go and plan your route around it.
The steps up Mount Caglago have little shade, so bring water and a hat and climb early in the morning.
Power outages are not uncommon, so it's a good idea to bring a power bank and a flashlight.
The Virgin Mary viewpoint on Mount Caglago (Tabgon Barangay) is reached by climbing 524 steps, and the statue, about 26 feet tall, opened on
. It is lit at night and serves as a guide for fishermen. Take breaks as you climb.
Environmental fees, island entrance fees, and tricycles require small change, so bring small bills of
, and
From
November–February
the sea can get rough and boats may be cancelled without notice, so it's recommended to be back in Naga the day before your return flight.
Always wear a life vest on the bangka, and don't push for the far-island route on days with high waves.
Access to some islands may be restricted during Survivor filming, so check the latest notices with your accommodation or the tourist information office.
Do not touch or take coral and starfish. Waste collection facilities are limited on each island, so take back any trash you bring in.
The sun is very strong, so bring reef-safe sunscreen and a rash guard, and pack plenty of water to guard against dehydration.
Agree clearly beforehand on the bangka fare and route — which islands are included, whether entrance fees are covered, and whether lunch is included — to avoid disputes later.
The Huyentebela national highway from Naga to Caramoan has sharp curves, unlit stretches, and coastal cliff roads, so it's safer to avoid driving at night and arrive before sunset.
